title: ⭐ Practice: at the edge of space

questions.prompt: Which idiom means "to travel to many different countries"?
questions.explanation: "To see the world" is the idiom for travelling widely, one country after another. "To do the sights" stays inside a single city: it is visiting its famous places in a day or two. "To get a foothold" is a business image — a first strong position in a market — and "to make a deal" is to reach an agreement. An idiom is never the sum of its words, which is why none of these can be built from see, do, sight or deal.

questions.prompt: An advertisement wants to say that its offer cannot be resisted. How is that adjective spelt?
questions.explanation: Before a word beginning with r, the negative prefix is written ir-, and neither the prefix nor the word loses a letter when they meet: ir + resistible gives irresistible, with a double r. Dropping one r is the commonest spelling slip of the whole family — compare illegal, illiterate and immature, which double their letter for exactly the same reason. Un- and in- are not available here, because the first letter of the word has already decided.

questions.prompt: At the boarding gate a hostess asks: "Would you mind ___ a few minutes? The shuttle is being refuelled." Which form fits?
questions.explanation: "Mind" is one of the verbs that must be followed by a verb in the -ing form: Would you mind waiting? The polite question really asks whether waiting is a problem for you, and the -ing form is what names that activity. The form with "to" copies would you like to wait, which is a different verb altogether, and neither the bare form nor the past form can follow mind.

questions.prompt: Four passengers said these words at the spaceport. Match each one with the sentence that reports what the speaker did.

options.text: "It wasn't me. I never touched the controls."
"Fine — I broke the rule, and I am sorry."
"Why don't we book the next flight instead?"
"We will travel next year, not this year."

questions.explanation: All four reporting verbs take a verb in the -ing form, so it is the meaning that sorts them out: to deny is to say you did not do something, to admit is to say you did, to suggest is to put an idea forward, and to postpone is to push an action to a later date. Notice that a report of this kind never keeps the speaker's own words — it names the act itself with an -ing form, and "he suggested to book" is impossible where "he suggested booking" is right.

questions.prompt: An article announces "2.5-hour flights to the edge of space". Which sentence says the same thing?

options.text: Each flight lasts two hours and five minutes.
Each flight lasts two hours and a half.
Each flight lasts two and a half days.

questions.explanation: In English the dot is the decimal point and is read "point": 2.5 is two point five, that is two and a half, so a 2.5-hour flight lasts two hours and thirty minutes. The dot does not separate hours from minutes — two hours and five minutes would be written 2.05 — and it never separates thousands either: that job belongs to the comma, as in 3,000,000. Many languages give the two marks the opposite roles, which is exactly where the mistake comes from.

questions.prompt: The rocket was ready, but the weather turned bad, so the company ___ launching its first tourist flight until the spring. Which verb fits the situation?
questions.explanation: All four verbs take a verb in the -ing form, so the grammar decides nothing here and the meaning must: to postpone is to move an action to a later date, which is precisely what "until the spring" announces. To regret launching would mean the flight had already gone up and the company was sorry about it; to practise launching is to repeat the operation in order to get better at it; and to deny launching is to claim the flight never took place at all.
